text: FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 10, 1926.

label: header
text: THE CHINA MAIL.

label: paragraph_title
text: BALANCE OF POWER

label: paragraph_title
text: China.

label: text
text: ALLIANCE AGAINST CANTON?

label: paragraph_title
text: Movements Against Nationalist Flank and Rear.

label: text
text: To preserve the balance of power in China, Marshal Sun Chuan-fang now seems decided that he must fight the Cantonese.

label: text
text: With the temporary eclipse of Marshal Wu Pei-fu, the position in China is not unlike that of the "Three Kingdoms" period—several centuries B.C.—when the third generation of the original disputants ultimately worked out their own salvation:

label: text
text: Only 18 months ago, Sun Chuanfang attacked the Fengtien party, driving them out from the Yangtse valley and back into Shantung. Now he seeks an alliance with Marshal Chang Tsolin, the leader of Fengtien.

label: text
text: Latest intelligence is that Sun Chuan-fang's five provinces are sending out an expedition to attack the Nationalist flank.

label: text
text: An earlier Rêuter cible from Shantung stated:—Various reports are current from Japanese and allegedly official sources to the effect that Wuchang has not surrendered to the southerners.

label: paragraph_title
text: Fengien, Alarmed.

label: text
text: Of this the only thing to be said is that there is little doubt and that another version may come to-morrow.

label: text
text: It was General Li Chung-jen's 7th army which entered Wuchang and Tang Sang-chi's 8th army took Hanyang. Anti-imperialist and anti-Japanese leaflets have been distributed.

label: text
text: A few days ago they promised heavy reinforcements but nothing more has been heard.

label: text
text: The Fengtien leaders are also considering an expedition towards Hankow to check the Cantonese.

label: text
text: Rivals in Touch.

label: text
text: Of principal interest at the moment is the fact that Sun Chuan-fang—who has become famous for a series of classical compositions—has decided on war. Couched in flowery language—the last message exceeded 500 words—he sent several ultimatum to Chang Kai-shek, giving him 24 hours to retire into Kwangtung, this being a physical impossibility.

label: text
text: The vanguard of the five provinces is reported to have met a detachment of the southern who had advanced to Pinghsiang in Kiangsi province. Tupan Lu Hsiang-ting, leading the new allies, is at Juichow, about 40 miles east of Nanchang (capital of Kiangsi) and close to the new war zone.

label: text
text: Tupan Chow Yam-yan of Fukien has announced his intention of establishing a base at Changchow, close to the Kwangtung border, for an offensive against the Nationalist home territory.

label: paragraph_title
text: "All is Safe."

label: paragraph_title
text: Shanghai, Sept. 10.

label: text
text: A report from Hankow on September 8 states that the allies had completely evacuated Han-yang and Hankow native city.

label: text
text:
Further fighting was at first feared but the evacuation was carried out peacefully, although it was reported that the retreating Northerners looted several villages on the outskirts of Hankow.
The situation here is remarkably quiet.

label: text
text: The Southerners launched another attack on Wuchang on the night of September 7, which was unsuccessful.

label: text
text: the walls indicate that all is safe. The Southerners at Hankow issued numerous proclamations, assuring the population of peace and protection and threatening evil-doers with execution.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: Steel Helmets for China!

label: text
text: The “Daily Mail” learns that a large consignment of British steel helmets were sent to China recently for use by Chinese soldiers.

label: text
text: Heimets used by British soldiers in the War were sold to a London firm who consigned 30,000 to Marshal Chang Tso-lin of Fengtien.

label: text
text: They stated that the helmets were required for “ornamental purposes.”—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: BRITISH POLICY.

label: paragraph_title
text: HOME PAPERS SPEAK ON CHINA

label: text
text: London, Sept. 9.

label: text
text: INACTIVITY TO GO?

label: text
text: The “Daily News,” in an editorial on the “Chinese Chaos” concludes as follows:—There is nothing to be done at present but to wait patiently for a chance to do something effective.

label: text
text: The “Daily Mail,” in a leader, says that amid the welter, it will be of little practical use to apply pressure to the helpless Government at Peking, yet it is clear that even Chinese generals and Communist republics cannot be permitted to go beyond certain limits in their behaviour towards foreign and friendly States.

label: text
text: Isolated intervention is rightly undesirable so long as it can be avoided, but some common policy may have to be concocted by Eastern and Western civilised Powers, which have joint and common interest in helping China to release herself from anarchy and misrule.

label: text
text: The “Daily Chronicle” urges the organisation of really efficient British propaganda in China.

label: text
text: The "Times," in a leader, says that the extension of civil war in China may force the Powers to agree to a common policy.

label: text
text: It will certainly oblige Britain to redouble its efforts to defend the rights and safety of its nationals in Chinese territory.

label: text
text: The report that Mr. Miles Lampson, who has imagination and personality, will be the next British Minister to Peking, may justify the hope that the British Government may soon be able to adopt a more positive policy in the Far East, where British inactivity has not always been masterly.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: OPIUM TRAFFIC.

label: text
text: APPEAL TO ITALIAN GOVERNMENT.

label: text
text: INDIA'S MEASURES:

label: text
text: Geneva, Sept. 9.

label: text
text: At a meeting of the Opium Traffic Committee, Lord Cecil appealed to the Italian member to urge the Italian Government to reconsider its decision and agree to sign the 1925 Geneva Convention.

label: text
text: Sir Kumar Mullick gave a detailed account of the measures taken by the Indian Government against the traffic in opium and dangerous drugs. He declared that India was carrying out the provisions of the Geneva and The Hague Conventions. He agreed with Lord Cecil as regards the necessity for an international agreement to control the export and use of deleterious drugs, and asked that the illicit drug traffic to India should be stopped.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: Egyptian Crop

label: text
text: The Government is buying the existing opium crop at £200,000, and hopes to find a purchaser for the whole crop. Poppy growing in Egypt will henceforth be prohibited.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: COMMUNISTS' TRIAL.

label: paragraph_title
text: LEADER SENTENCED TO EIGHT YEARS.

label: text
text: ASSOCIATES CONVICTED.

label: text
text: Abramson, the leader of the New Workers' Party and Socialist ex-Member of Parliament, who was arrested on April 20 when is alleged to have been receiving instructions from a representative of the Moscow International, who was conducting a Communist propaganda in Estonia, has been sentenced to eight years' penal servitude.

label: text
text: Four of K's associates were sentenced to penal servitude for terms ranging from three to ten years.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: FEUD IN GREECE.

label: paragraph_title
text: GUARD SURRENDER.

label: paragraph_title
text: Athèns; September 9.

label: text
text: An armed mob attacked the Central Telegraph office and exchanged many shots with the military guard. It is feared that there were many casualties in the streets.—Reuter.

label: text
text: It is semi-officially announced that M. Kondylis's Government's order for the disbandment of the Republican Guard was carried out this morning. The Guard, which is a separate force and independent of the Army, was founded by General Pangafos in order to support his dictatorship. It refused to obey the order to lay down arms and consequently the Government called on the Regular army. After a few hours' skirmishing, in which a few casualties occurred, the guard surrendered unconditionally.—Reuter. Athens, later.

label: text
text: Order has been restored. It is reported that 40 were killed and 100 wounded in the street fighting.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: TRADE UNIONS.

label: text
text: POSITION IN HONG KONG AND SHANGHAI.

label: text
text: NO AUTHENTIC INFORMATION

label: text
text: London, Sept. 9.

label: text
text: At the Trade Union Congress, the Secretary, Mr. Citrine, replying to criticism of the General Council's report on the Trade Union situation in Hong Kong and Shanghai, said that they had received information from various sources to the effect that there were approximately 300 separate Trade Unions in those areas, but they were unable to authenticate that information, and as to the suppression of Unions in Shanghai there was evidence that Trade Unionism there was practically non-existent.—Reuter.

label: text
text: Reuter

label: text
text: London, later.

label: text
text: The Trade Union Congress at Bournemouth rejected a motion for reference back of the General Council's report on Trade Unionism in China. The mover of the motion referred to the suppression of Trade Unions in Shanghai and said that the only place in China where Trade Unionism flourishes was Canton.

label: paragraph_title
text: FRANC FALLS.

label: paragraph_title
text: NO ALARM CREATED IN PARIS.

label: text
text: SIMPLE EXPLANATION.

label: text
text: Paris, September 9.

label: text
text: The sudden fall of the franc from 164.40 yesterday to 169.65 to-day is not regarded here as abnormal.

label: text
text: It is attributed to the fact that traders are buying appreciated currencies in order to cover themselves before the tide of the Autumn trade sets in.

label: text
text: It is stated that over a million dollars were bought on behalf of wheat importers.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: TRAIN DERAILED:

label: paragraph_title
text: THREE PERSONS KILLED IN HOLLAND.

label: text
text: TEN SERIOUSLY INJURED

label: text
text: The Hague, Sept. 9.

label: text
text: Three persons were killed, and 10 seriously injured and a number slightly injured as the result of the derailing of a passenger train near Leyden—Reuter.

label: text
text:
The Hague, Later.
The killed in the railway derailment at Leyden include Lobo Brakensiek and his wife, the well-known Amsterdam actress.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: REBEL'S DEFEAT.

label: text
text:
SEVEN-HOURS' BATTLE IN
NICARAGUA.

label: text
text: GENERAL KILLED.

label: text
text:
Managua, September 9.
A seven-hours' battle at Somotillo resulted in the defeat of 800 Nicaraguan revolutionaries with the loss of 30 killed, including General Pedro Grillo, and 50 wounded.
The Government losses were eight killed and 20 wounded.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: A day behind her fixed hour of departure, the B. & I. liner "Talamba" left port this morning with cargo and passengers for Amoy. She is later proceeding to Shanghai and Japan. The "Talamba" also took mail for her ports of call.

label: text
text: Early this morning, the Dollar Inner "President Pierce" arrived from Manila with 16 first cabin passengers for Hongkong and 20 through passengers. She also brought about 336 tons of general cargo for discharge here, besides Manila majl. The "Pierce" will leave for San Francisco on Sunday at noon.

label: text
text: The local office of the Messageries Maritimes will despatch their steamer "Tonkin" for Haiphong this afternoon with cargo and mail only. The "Tonkin" arrived this morning from Haiphong with about 300 tons of general cargo for discharge here.

label: text
text: The Standard Oil Co. despatched their tanker s.s. "Tascalusa" for her return trip to San Francisco, where she will loan oil for the Company here.

label: text
text: Bound for Marscilles, London and Hamburg, the P. & O. liner “Nagpore” leaves this afternoon with passengers, cargo and mail for Europe.

label: text
text: * 场

label: text
text: From the Japanese ports the s.s. "Chicago Maru" arrived yesterday afternoon with 292 tons of cargo mostly consisting of safety matches for discharge here. The "Chicago Maru" will be despatched for East Africa this afternoon.

label: text
text: The German steamer "Trier" arrived early this morning from Hamburg via Singapore with 550 tons of cargo and only 3 saloon passengers for Hongkong. She will leave for Shanghai to tomorrow morning at daylight.

label: text
text: Two of the Indo-China Navigation Company's steamers will leave port to-morrow.—the s.s. "Haying" bound for Bangkok, and the s.s. "Sinkiang" bound for Shanghai direct. Both steamers are taking cargo and deck passengers.

label: text
text: The local office of the Admiral Oriental line has been advised by their Manila office, that they will despatch the s.s. "President Grant" from that port for Seattle via Hong Kong. The "Grant" is due to arrive here on Sunday morning at daylight.

label: paragraph_title
text: DICK NORTON COMING.

label: text
text:
The “China Mail” is informed that Mr. “Dick” Norton and his “Globetrotters” are due to open in Hong Kong on October 3. This talented company are due to leave Penang to-day for Bangkok where they will play prior to sailing for Hong Kong.
Miss Lola Forbes (Mrs. Norton) has been visiting New Zealand since the Company were last in the Colony and if present arrangements are carried out, she will rejoin the Company when they arrive in Hong Kong.

label: paragraph_title
text: CORRESPONDENCE.

label: text
text: SOVIET INTERFERENCE WITH BRITISH TRADE.

label: text
text:
[To the Editor of the “China Mail.”]
Sir,—Most sober-minded Britons will have read with interest the report of the Albert Hall mass meeting of protest against Soviet interference with British affairs, which was published in Wednesday's issue of the “China Mail.”

label: text
text: Commander' Locker-Lampson's very pertinent observations will, it is to be hoped, carry some weight with the Imperial Government, but it is of Soviet interference with British affairs in China that people whose lot it is to be domiciled in the Far East are more particularly concerned.

label: text
text: Sir Reginald Stubbs did not hesitate in making it perfectly clear that the Soviet Government was directly behind the boycott and strike—in fact it might almost be said that Sir Reginald never lost an opportunity for explaining this fact and his firm handed policy when dealing with the menace last summer was unquestionably fully justified.

label: text
text: Sir Austen Chamberlain and Mr. Ronald McNeill have both stated that the Government had reason to believe that "outside influences were at work" and Mr. Locker-Lampson, the present Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, has stated that "evidence has been received that the Soviet Government in China and elsewhere was not observing the terms of the Russo-British Trading Agreement whereby it undertook not to carry on or support anti-British propaganda."

label: text
text: The Imperial Government may be perfectly right in its belief that abrogation of the Russo-British Agreement would serve no useful purpose, but surely it is about time that something was done in the matter? Here we are some fourteen months after the Shanghai emeute of May 30, 1925 and subsequent upheaval in South China and yet all efforts on the part of the Colonial Government have proved in vain. There is direct evidence to lead us to believe that the merchants of Canton are anxious to have the matter settled, but, owing to the mischief-making activities of the Strike Committee, backed by the so-called Nationalist Government, all efforts have proved fruitless.

label: text
text: It is quite obvious that all efforts on the part of the British Minister in Peking will be useless. Peking has no more control over Canton than has Sofia over Monrovia. It is not with the Canton Government nor with the so-called Peking Government that the British Government should deal. Surely it is with Moscow that the British protest should be lodged? Is, one is tempted to ask, the Imperial Government being completely hoodwinked by reported vast orders that Moscow is alleged to be placing with Britain? Is British trade and prestige in the Far East to be sacrificed in order that Manchester, Bradford and Sheffield may secure their share of the contemplated orders that Moscow is said to be placing abroad? Let us hope that the appointment of a new Minister in Peking will mean the advent of a new and firmer policy. The atmosphere is literally charged with rumours of war. Had Britain declared war on Soviet propaganda and direct interference with British trade a year ago, we should not be where we are to day. As it is, all we can do it to nestle in our snug little island and watch events in the Yangtze Valley.
